extraction_text: Kings gathered in Kalinga for the svayamvara (self-choice ceremony) of Princess Bhanumati.

attributes.relationship: Allies

extraction_text: Princess Bhanumati passed by Duryodhana without stopping during the ceremony.
Duryodhana, enraged by the rejection, abducted Princess Bhanumati in his chariot, challenging the other kings.
Karna, armed and in a chariot, protected Duryodhana by fighting off the attacking kings.
Karna defeated the kings, disrupting their forces and killing many charioteers, causing them to flee.
Duryodhana, under Karna's protection, returned to Hastinapura happily with Princess Bhanumati.

attributes.relationship: Karna as protector to Duryodhana

extraction_text: King Jarasandha of Magadha, hearing of Karna's prowess, challenged him to a single combat.
Karna and Jarasandha fought using various weapons until their resources were exhausted, then engaged in hand-to-hand combat.
Karna struck Jarasandha with such force that it affected Jarasandha's uniquely joined body.
Duryodhana gave the city of Malini to Karna and made him king of Anga and Champa.

attributes.relationship_change: Duryodhana elevates Karna's status from king of Anga to also ruler of Champa.

extraction_text: Indra, disguised by divine illusion, asked Karna for his innate earrings and armor.
Karna, deceived by the divine illusion, gave away his innate earrings and armor.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Karna loses his divine, innate protections.

extraction_text: Karna was killed by Arjuna in the presence of Krishna.

attributes.reason: Multiple factors contributed: curses from a Brahmin and Parashurama, a boon granted to Kunti, Indra's illusion, Bhishma's contempt, Shalya diminishing his power, and Krishna's strategy.

extraction_text: Arjuna acquired divine weapons from various gods (Rudra, Indra, Yama, Varuna, Kubera, Drona, and Kripa) and used them to kill Karna.

attributes.action: Acquisition and use of divine weapons

extraction_text: Arjuna criticizes Yudhishthira's decision, questioning why he would foolishly abandon the supreme prosperity won by killing enemies and conquering the earth through dharma.

attributes.relationship: Younger brother (Arjuna) challenges the elder's (Yudhishthira) renunciation plan.

extraction_text: A person willing to beg for food will not take any action to pursue career success.
The speaker criticizes the king for wanting to adopt the evil Kapila lifestyle, abandoning his prosperous kingdom.

attributes.relationship: Advisor to king

extraction_text: The speaker questions why the king wants to abandon all undertakings, wealth, and live like a beggar in the forest.
The speaker argues that abandoning everything would allow evil people to ruin sacrifices and cause sin.
The speaker quotes Nahusha saying 'Poverty is despair' and criticizes poverty.
The speaker argues that righteousness depends on wealth, and seizing someone's wealth seizes their righteousness.
The speaker describes how everything - righteousness, love, heaven, knowledge, self-control - originates from wealth.
The speaker argues that without wealth, one cannot perform rituals properly.
The speaker asks the king to consider how gods prospered by killing their relatives (the Asuras).
The speaker concludes that wealth must be acquired, and this is how kings win the earth.
A king (likely Yudhishthira, based on context of winning the earth and being addressed about performing a sacrifice) is told by the royal sages (Pitris) that the earth he won is not truly his alone.

attributes.relationship: The sages are instructing the king on royal duty (Dharma).

extraction_text: The sages explain that wealth from the king's treasury flows to the earth like water from the ocean, and that the earth previously belonged to kings like Dilipa, Nighna, Yuvinashva, Ambarisha, and Mandhata.
The sages declare that a grand and generous sacrifice (likely the Ashvamedha or Rajasuya) awaits Yudhishthira, and that failing to perform it would offend the gods.

attributes.relationship_change: Establishes a religious obligation for the king.

extraction_text: The sages describe how a king's performance of the horse sacrifice purifies his subjects.
The sages reference the cosmic sacrifice performed by the Supreme Being (Vishnu/Shiva as Viraj), where all beings and Himself are the offering.

attributes.supernatural_element: Description of a divine, universal sacrifice.

extraction_text: The sages conclude by calling this the eternal, auspicious, and endless path—the 'Dasharatha' (ten-charioted) highway—and urge the king not to stray from it.

attributes.relationship: The sages act as spiritual guides defining the king's Dharma.
